title: Hebrew and Aramaic for reading
principle: Language is learned as a reading instrument: every form should help a learner make a better move in a real source.

stages.title: Orient to the page
stages.goal: Recognize Hebrew direction, common marks, and the difference between a name, a question, and a source signal.
stages.mastery: Correctly classify three page signals in two separate source contexts.

items.source: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 begins with this word.
items.prompt: What should a reader expect after this word?
answers: A question about a starting point in time.
A final ruling without an argument.

items.source: Torah narratives commonly use this verb before speech.
answers: It introduces speech by a speaker.

items.source: Gemara uses this signal when bringing a tannaitic teaching.
items.prompt: What should you look for next?
answers: A cited teaching that can clarify or test the discussion.
A personal instruction to the learner.

stages.title: Hear the argument signals
stages.goal: Recognize the small words that tell you a sugya is asking, citing, or objecting.
stages.mastery: Predict the next move after a signal in an unfamiliar mini-source.

items.transliteration: mai — what? / what is the meaning?
items.source: Gemara often stops and asks this about a word or statement.
items.prompt: What reading move is being requested?
answers: Clarify what a word or claim means.

items.source: A verse is about to enter the discussion as evidence.
items.prompt: What should a reader expect next?
answers: A biblical text used as evidence.

items.source: A source puts pressure on an earlier claim.
items.prompt: What is the source doing here?
answers: Testing whether the preceding claim can stand.
Repeating the same claim for emphasis.

stages.title: Read reusable phrase templates
stages.goal: Treat high-frequency phrases as meaningful units rather than isolated letters.
stages.mastery: Identify the argumentative job of a phrase before opening its translation.

items.source: Gemara invites a source into the question under discussion.
items.prompt: What is this phrase asking the reader to do?
answers: Examine a source as possible evidence.
Translate a word into another language.

items.transliteration: la kashya — it is not difficult
items.source: A distinction may resolve an apparent conflict.
items.prompt: What should you look for after this phrase?
answers: A reason the two sources can both be true.

items.source: The discussion draws an inference from what has been established.
answers: A conclusion is being drawn from the source.
A question about time is beginning.

stages.title: Locate roles in a sentence
stages.goal: Find the actor, action, object, and connector before attempting a polished translation.
stages.mastery: Give a role-map for two short Hebrew or Aramaic sentences.

items.source: A common attribution frame in rabbinic literature.
items.prompt: Which role does the final word fill?

items.transliteration: hakhi ka'amar — this is what it means
items.source: A Gemara response reframes how to read an earlier statement.
answers: Explaining the intended meaning of an earlier statement.

items.source: A compact turn in the line of reasoning.
items.prompt: What should the reader watch for?
answers: A correction or redirection in the argument.

stages.title: Read an unfamiliar mini-sugya
stages.goal: Use signals, phrase templates, and sentence roles to make a first independent map of a short passage.
stages.mastery: Label a question, source, and answer move in an unfamiliar passage, then use translation to check rather than replace the map.

items.transliteration: ibaya lehu — they raised a question
items.source: The Gemara introduces a focused inquiry for examination.
items.prompt: What should a learner expect after this phrase?

items.transliteration: gufa — returning to the statement itself
items.source: After a detour, the Gemara returns to study an earlier teaching.
items.prompt: How should this change your map of the sugya?
answers: Reconnect the present line to an earlier statement.
Assume the topic has changed completely.

items.source: Some tensions remain open or require more study.
answers: Keep the difficulty visible; do not pretend it has been solved.
Treat it as a personal legal ruling.
Skip directly to the next tractate.
